derivations.claim: Let $(x^{(k)})_{k\ge1}$ be Cauchy in $\ell^2(\mathbb N_0,\mathbb C)$. For each fixed $n$, $|x_n^{(k)}-x_n^{(\ell)}|\le\|x^{(k)}-x^{(\ell)}\|_2$, so [F2] gives a unique coordinate limit $x_n$. The sequence is norm-bounded: choose $k_0$ so that $\|x^{(k)}-x^{(k_0)}\|_2<1$ for $k\ge k_0$, bound those terms by $1+\|x^{(k_0)}\|_2$, and enlarge the bound to include the finitely many earlier norms. Call the resulting bound $C$. For every finite $F\subseteq\mathbb N_0$, finite-sum continuity gives $\sum_{n\in F}|x_n|^2=\lim_k\sum_{n\in F}|x_n^{(k)}|^2\le C^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x\in\ell^2$.

Given $\delta>0$, choose $k_1$ so $\|x^{(k)}-x^{(\ell)}\|_2<\delta/2$ whenever $k,\ell\ge k_1$. Fix $k\ge k_1$. For each finite $F$, coordinate convergence and the finite sum imply $\sum_{n\in F}|x_n^{(k)}-x_n|^2=\lim_{\ell\to\infty}\sum_{n\in F}|x_n^{(k)}-x_n^{(\ell)}|^2\le(\delta/2)^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ gives $\|x^{(k)}-x\|_2\le\delta/2<\delta$. Thus every Cauchy sequence converges in this norm; [F3] gives the Hilbert-space conclusion. The coordinate limits are uniquely determined, so no choice principle is used.

Therefore $\beta_i=1/(k_BT_i)=N_i\beta_K$, and the local grand generator $G_i:=N_i(H_i-\mu_iQ_i)$ satisfies $G_i=N_iH_i+(q\Phi_i-\mu_K)Q_i$. Summing this identity gives $G_K=\sum_iG_i=H_K-\mu_KQ$.

Each pair $H_i,Q_i$ is simultaneously diagonalizable: diagonalize $Q_i$ using [F1]; each eigenspace of $Q_i$ is invariant under $H_i$ because $H_iQ_i=Q_iH_i$; diagonalize the Hermitian restriction of $H_i$ on each of the finitely many eigenspaces. The resulting orthonormal basis of $\mathcal H_i$ diagonalizes $G_i$. The tensor products of these bases form an orthonormal basis of $\mathcal H$, and in that basis $G_K=\sum_iG_i$ has eigenvalue $\sum_i g_{i,a_i}$ on the basis vector indexed by $(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$.

The finite trace in that product basis is $$Z=\sum_{a_1,\ldots,a_r}\prod_{i=1}^r e^{-\beta_Kg_{i,a_i}}=\prod_{i=1}^r\left(\sum_{a_i}e^{-\beta_Kg_{i,a_i}}\right)=\prod_{i=1}^rZ_i.$$ Each factor is a finite sum of strictly positive reals, so $0<Z_i<\infty$ and $0<Z<\infty$. Dividing each diagonal weight by this product gives $\rho=\bigotimes_i Z_i^{-1}e^{-\beta_KG_i}=\bigotimes_i\rho_i$, and $\beta_KG_i=\beta_i(H_i-\mu_iQ_i)$.
Apply [F2] to the finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix $G_K$ and $\beta_K>0$: $\rho$ is a state and is KMS for $\alpha^G_t(B)=e^{itG_K/\hbar}Be^{-itG_K/\hbar}$ on $\mathcal B(\mathcal H)$.

Since $[H_K,Q]=0$, the exponentials of these two matrices commute and $e^{itG_K/\hbar}=e^{itH_K/\hbar}e^{-it\mu_KQ/\hbar}$. For $B\in\mathcal A_0$, $B$ commutes with $Q$, so $\alpha^G_t(B)=e^{itH_K/\hbar}Be^{-itH_K/\hbar}=:\alpha^H_t(B)$. The algebra $\mathcal A_0$ is closed under products, adjoints and linear combinations and is invariant under $\alpha^H_t$. Restricting the state and the same bounded strip functions from step 4.1 to $A,B\in\mathcal A_0$ proves the physical $H_K$ KMS condition there. No KMS claim for charged observables is made.

derivations.claim: For $A,B\in\mathcal A$, let $F_{A,B}$ be the strip function supplied by [F1]. Define $\widetilde F_{A,B}(z):=F_{A,B}(z/\lambda)$. If $0\le\operatorname{Im}z\le\lambda\beta_K\hbar$, then $0\le\operatorname{Im}(z/\lambda)\le\beta_K\hbar$; hence $\widetilde F$ is bounded and continuous on the rescaled closed strip and holomorphic inside. For real $\tau$, $\widetilde F_{A,B}(\tau)=\omega(A\alpha_{\tau/\lambda}(B))=\omega(A\alpha^\lambda_\tau(B))$, and at the upper edge $\widetilde F_{A,B}(\tau+i\lambda\beta_K\hbar)=\omega(\alpha^\lambda_\tau(B)A)$. Thus it is the required $\lambda\beta_K$-KMS function.

Conversely, if $\widetilde F_{A,B}$ witnesses the $\widehat\beta$-KMS property for $\alpha^\lambda$, define $G_{A,B}(z):=\widetilde F_{A,B}(\lambda z)$. Positive $\lambda$ maps the strip of width $(\widehat\beta/\lambda)\hbar$ to the strip of width $\widehat\beta\hbar$, so boundedness, boundary continuity and interior holomorphy are preserved. The lower edge is $\omega(A\alpha^\lambda_{\lambda t}(B))=\omega(A\alpha_t(B))$, and the upper edge is $\omega(\alpha_t(B)A)$. This proves the converse.

On a stationary orbit, [F2] makes $N$ constant along its Killing flow and gives $T_{\mathrm{loc}}=T_K/N$. Therefore $(k_BT_{\mathrm{loc}})^{-1}=N(k_BT_K)^{-1}=N\beta_K$, exactly the inverse-temperature scaling proved in step 1.1 when $\lambda=N$. The result applies separately on each orbit; it constructs no global automorphism with position-dependent rescaling.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}=N\beta_K$ and $\sigma$ is the same normalized density for $G_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and $G_K=NG_{\mathrm{loc}}$. For neutral matrices the chemical term proportional to $Q$ does not change conjugation, so $\alpha^K_t(A)=\alpha^{\mathrm{loc}}_{Nt}(A)$ and the same holds for $B$.

If $U_{\mathrm{loc}}(\tau)$ solves $i\hbar U'_{\mathrm{loc}}=(G_{\mathrm{loc}}-\epsilon h(\tau)B)U_{\mathrm{loc}}$, then the chain rule gives $$i\hbar\frac{d}{dt}U_{\mathrm{loc}}(Nt)=\bigl(G_K-\epsilon N h(Nt)B\bigr)U_{\mathrm{loc}}(Nt).$$ Both grand-generator propagators have the same identity initial condition. Uniqueness of the finite-dimensional controlled evolution in [F2] gives $U_K(t)=U_{\mathrm{loc}}(Nt)$ and equality of the grand-generator expectations. To compare with the physical controls, note that $H_{\mathrm{loc}}=G_{\mathrm{loc}}+\mu_{\mathrm{loc}}Q$ and $H_K=G_K+\mu_KQ$. Each grand controlled generator commutes with $Q$ at every time because $[G_{\mathrm{loc}},Q]=[B,Q]=0$. Therefore the corresponding physical propagator equals its grand propagator multiplied by $e^{-i\mu_{\mathrm{loc}}Q\tau/\hbar}$ locally or $e^{-i\mu_KQt/\hbar}$ in Killing time; differentiating these products verifies their evolution equations and identity initial data. Since $[A,Q]=0$, conjugation by these extra factors leaves $A$ fixed, so physical and grand expectations agree. The two exact expectation equalities imply $E_K(t)=E_{\mathrm{loc}}(Nt)$.

Apply [F2] on $[0,S]$ locally and on $[0,S/N]$ in Killing time. Its Killing kernel is $R_K(t)=R_{\mathrm{loc}}(Nt)$ by step 1.1. The first-order terms agree because $$\epsilon\int_0^tNh(Ns)R_{\mathrm{loc}}(N(t-s))\,ds=\epsilon\int_0^{Nt}h(v)R_{\mathrm{loc}}(Nt-v)\,dv$$ after $v=Ns$. Also $$\frac2\hbar\int_0^{S/N}|Nh(Ns)|\|B\|\,ds=C_S,$$ so the two Kubo remainder bounds agree at corresponding times.

Diagonalize $G_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with eigenvalues $E_j$ and eigenvectors $u_j$. The density weights $p_j=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}E_j}$ are also the weights for $G_K$, whose eigenvalues are $NE_j$; hence each transition frequency is multiplied by $N$, while each weight and matrix element of $A$ is unchanged. By [F3], $S_K=(D_N)_*S_{\mathrm{loc}}$, equivalently the displayed distribution scaling. Since $\beta_K\hbar N\omega=\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}\hbar\omega$, detailed balance is preserved; $D_N(0)=0$ carries any zero-frequency atom to itself, where [F3] gives no coth formula.

Apply [F4] to the local re-prepared density $\sigma_\lambda\propto e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(G_{\mathrm{loc}}-\lambda B)}$ to obtain the stated Kubo–Mori derivative. Since $G_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is finite Hermitian and $x\mapsto e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}x}$ is injective on its real spectrum, $B$ commutes with $\sigma$ exactly when it commutes with $G_{\mathrm{loc}}$ (both preserve the same eigenspace decomposition). Thus the variance reduction in [F4] has precisely the condition stated here; the finite-time expansion in step 2.2 instead keeps the initial $\sigma$ fixed.

derivations.claim: By [F3], $\mathcal H$ with the displayed inner product is complete, so it is a Hilbert space. Finite-support sequences lie in $D(\mathcal N)$ and are dense in $\mathcal H$: for any $x\in\mathcal H$, the finite partial sums of $\sum_n|x_n|^2$ increase to its finite supremum, so the squared norm of the truncation tail tends to zero. Hence $\mathcal N$ is densely defined. For $x,y\in D(\mathcal N)$, Cauchy–Schwarz [F2] gives convergence of both inner-product sums and $$\langle \mathcal Nx,y\rangle=\sum_n nx_n\overline{y_n}=\sum_n x_n\overline{ny_n}=\langle x,\mathcal Ny\rangle,$$ so the operator is symmetric.

On the basis vector $e_n$, the Gibbs weight for $K$ is $e^{-\beta_Kan}$, so the partition sum is the displayed nonnegative series. If $a>0$, put $r=e^{-\beta_Ka}\in(0,1)$; its partial sums are $(1-r^{M+1})/(1-r)$ and tend to $(1-r)^{-1}$. If $a=0$, every term is $1$ and the partial sums tend to $+\infty$. If $a<0$, the terms $e^{\beta_K|a|n}$ do not tend to zero, so the nonnegative series diverges.

If $y\in D(\mathcal N)$, then $z:=\mathcal Ny\in\mathcal H$, and step 1.1 shows $\langle\mathcal Nx,y\rangle=\langle x,z\rangle$ for every $x\in D(\mathcal N)$; thus $y\in D(\mathcal N^\dagger)$ and $\mathcal N^\dagger y=\mathcal Ny$. Conversely, if $y\in D(\mathcal N^\dagger)$ with representing vector $z\in\mathcal H$, test the defining identity on each $x=e_n$ to obtain $z_n=ny_n$. Since $z$ is square-summable, $\sum_n n^2|y_n|^2<\infty$, so $y\in D(\mathcal N)$ and $z=\mathcal Ny$. Therefore $D(\mathcal N^\dagger)=D(\mathcal N)$ and $\mathcal N^\dagger=\mathcal N$.

Multiplication by a real nonzero scalar $c$ leaves the adjoint domain $D(\mathcal N)$ unchanged and multiplies the adjoint action by $c$: the same coordinate test as step 2.1 forces $z_n=cn y_n$, and $(cn y_n)_n$ is square-summable exactly when $(ny_n)_n$ is. Thus $c\mathcal N$ is self-adjoint on $D(\mathcal N)$. The zero operator on all of $\mathcal H$ is self-adjoint: its adjoint relation forces $\langle x,z\rangle=0$ for every $x\in\mathcal H$, in particular $x=z$, so $z=0$. Taking $c=\epsilon$ and $c=\hbar m$ when $m\ne0$ proves the assertions for $H$ and $J$; when $m=0$, $J=0$ on all of $\mathcal H$. On the common domain, $K_0=a\mathcal N$. If $a\ne0$, this operator is self-adjoint and closed by the scalar argument, so its closure is itself. If $a=0$, $K_0$ is zero on the dense finite-support domain $D(\mathcal N)$; its graph closure is $\mathcal H\times\{0\}$ and hence $K$ is zero on all of $\mathcal H$, which is self-adjoint.

In the finite case $a>0$, $p_n=(1-r)r^n$ are positive and sum to one. For each bounded operator $B$, $\omega(B):=\sum_n p_n\langle Be_n,e_n\rangle$ converges absolutely because $|\langle Be_n,e_n\rangle|\le\|B\|$; it is normalized, linear and positive, since for any $C$, $\omega(C^*C)=\sum_n p_n\|Ce_n\|^2\ge0$. If $a\le0$, step 1.2 gives no finite normalizer for these same occupation weights. This proves exactly the asserted trace-Gibbs obstruction without any field-theoretic or spacetime extension.

derivations.claim: The eigenvectors of $Z$ have energies $+\Delta/2$ and $-\Delta/2$. Therefore $\operatorname{Tr}(e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}H_{\mathrm{loc}}})=e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}\Delta/2}+e^{\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}\Delta/2}=2\cosh(\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}\Delta/2)$, and $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma Z)=p_+-p_-=-\tanh(\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}\Delta/2)$.

With $\theta=\Delta\tau/\hbar$, direct multiplication using [L1] gives $e^{iH_{\mathrm{loc}}\tau/\hbar}Xe^{-iH_{\mathrm{loc}}\tau/\hbar}=X\cos\theta-Y\sin\theta$. Thus $[\alpha^{\mathrm{loc}}_\tau(X),X]=-\sin\theta[Y,X]=2iZ\sin\theta$, so the Kubo definition gives $R_{\mathrm{loc}}(\tau)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma[\alpha^{\mathrm{loc}}_\tau(X),X])=\frac{2}{\hbar}\tanh(\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}\Delta/2)\sin\theta$.

The only nonzero matrix elements of $X$ in the $Z$ eigenbasis exchange the two energy eigenvectors, so the two transition frequencies are $-\Delta/\hbar$ from the $+$ state and $+\Delta/\hbar$ from the $-$ state. Their Gibbs weights are $p_+$ and $p_-$ from step 1.1; hence the stated two-line spectral measure follows from the finite spectral expansion. The cell theorem sends each frequency $\omega$ to $N\omega$ without changing its weight, giving the Killing-time lines and periods in the Example.

Put $R(\lambda)=\sqrt{(\Delta/2)^2+\lambda^2}$. Since $H_{\mathrm{loc}}-\lambda X=(\Delta Z/2-\lambda X)$ and $ZX+XZ=0$ by [L1], its square is $R(\lambda)^2I$, so $$e^{-\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}(H_{\mathrm{loc}}-\lambda X)}=\cosh(\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}R(\lambda))I-\frac{\sinh(\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}R(\lambda))}{R(\lambda)}(H_{\mathrm{loc}}-\lambda X).$$ Taking traces and using $\operatorname{Tr}(H_{\mathrm{loc}}X)=0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(X^2)=2$ from [L1] gives $$\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma_\lambda X)=\lambda\frac{\tanh(\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}R(\lambda))}{R(\lambda)}.$$ Differentiating this explicit scalar expression at $\lambda=0$ yields the displayed static susceptibility. It is a derivative of a newly normalized Gibbs family, whereas the finite-time Kubo response in step 2.1 keeps $\sigma$ fixed.

Since $R_K(t)$ is a nonzero sinusoid when $\beta_{\mathrm{loc}}>0$ and $\Delta>0$, it is periodic and does not decay as $t\to\infty$. The theorem supplies no absolute-integrability hypothesis for a Green–Kubo limit, so the oscillatory finite response cannot be relabelled as a dc transport coefficient.
